/education/2026/oct/04/child-on-child-se.headline: Two-year waiting times highlight NHS struggle with rise in ADHD and autism awareness
/education/2026/oct/04/child-on-child-se.excerpt: That NHS boards have imposed minimum two-year waiting times for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism assessments shows a health service struggling to deal with the consequences of huge changes in understanding of and social attitudes to these conditions. Sharp rises in referrals for clinical assessments over the past six years mean nearly 1 million people in England are on ADHD waiting lists, with the average wait already over a year (64 weeks). About 295,000 await an autism assessment. Formal diagnosis has grown in recent years, slowly from the early 2000s and rapidly since 2020. Between 2020 and 2022, annual incidence of autism diagnosis in three- to 25-year-old males rose from 185 to 580 per 100,000, and from 45 to 320 in females. The lengthening waiting lists tell a tale not only of an NHS under financial strain and short of key staff, but also one of deepening distress for many patients and families for whom diagnosis is the key to clinical treatment and other forms of support. The explosion in diagnosis reflects the role of the NHS as a crucial gateway for a range of social support. If assessment bottlenecks mean it cannot deliver timely clinical assessments, this has serious knock-on effects; delays not just in medical help but in access to specialist support in schools or financial support through disability benefits.
/education/2026/oct/04/child-on-child-se.trail: NHS assessment bottlenecks have knock-on effects, leading to delays in medical help and lack of access to specialist support

/education/2026/oct/04/child-on-child-se.headline: The students returning to school after sexual assault: ‘You go back the next day, and you just deal with it’
/education/2026/oct/04/child-on-child-se.excerpt: In the wake of the latest headlines about alleged sexual assaults involving schoolboys and the death of a 16-year-old girl from suspected sexual choking, the national cabinet has agreed to prioritise its plan to end sexual violence against women, the New South Wales government has flagged a new set of priorities with education ministers and the federal government has announced draft legislation for a digital duty of care. Meanwhile, the victim at the centre of an alleged gang-rape involving two students from a Sydney private school and another boy has prepared to sit her HSC exams. “I can’t imagine what she is going through,” a police prosecutor, Sgt Rhonda Riley, told the court last month. “But she will need to complete her HSC going through pain and fear – not only mentally – for some time going forward.” As peer-on-peer violence continues to rise, many girls, who make up the majority of school-age sexual assault victims, have no choice but to return to school to continue their education in the shadow of their assault. And in many cases, they must continue to share a campus with their assailant. “In previous generations, it was more common for child sexual abuse to be inflicted by an adult than an adolescent,” reports the 2023 Australian Child Maltreatment Study.
/education/2026/oct/04/child-on-child-se.trail: Peer-on-peer violence is on the rise. But when schools must balance a duty of care to both victims and perpetrators, where does this leave girls who have to pursue their education in the shadow of sexual assault?

/education/2026/oct/04/child-on-child-se.headline: Northern Ireland schools must give girls option to wear trousers from next year
/education/2026/oct/04/child-on-child-se.excerpt: Schools in Northern Ireland must give girls the choice to wear trousers as part of their uniforms as well as for PE and games, according to revised guidelines. From next year schools would no longer be able to prohibit female pupils from wearing trousers, Paul Givan, the country’s education minister, said on Friday. “Today, I am taking that decision, that will be formally communicated, schools will be hearing from me,” he told the BBC. A law passed last year that was aimed at reducing the cost of uniforms gave girls the legal right to challenge schools that banned them from wearing trousers. However, campaigners said the change did not go far enough and put pressure on Givan, a Democratic Unionist party member of the Northern Ireland assembly (MLA) who said his own daughters wore skirts to school, to revise the guidelines. Givan said he had to strike a balance between schools’ autonomy and the level of prescription in departmental guidelines. “I have listened carefully over recent months to young people and the message is clear: girls want the choice to wear trousers as part of their school uniform.” The revised guidelines would not go into immediate effect to give schools time to update their policies, said Givan. Other parties welcomed the change but accused the education minister of dragging his feet.
/education/2026/oct/04/child-on-child-se.trail: DUP education minister accused of dragging feet before revising guidelines on uniform

/education/2026/oct/04/child-on-child-se.headline: Pupils with Send plans in England likely to double to one in 10 in rush for support
/education/2026/oct/04/child-on-child-se.excerpt: Schools and councils across England are expecting the proportion of children with special needs plans to double to one in 10, with families rushing to secure support before ministers bring in changes. Headteachers have reported an “unreal” surge in applications for education, health and care plans (EHCPs) mandating support for needs or disabilities such as speech and learning difficulties, autism or ADHD. In 2025, just one in 20 school-age children had EHCPs. The number of pupils with EHCPs has risen by more than 11% in each of the past two years, and projections by local authorities seen by the Guardian are anticipating similar double-digit annual increases over the next three years. Similar levels nationally would mean just under 10% of all school-age children with an EHCP in 2029. Such a rapid increase would outstrip the government’s own forecasts and eat into funding for improving specialist support in mainstream schools, undermining its plans for immediate reform while straining school and council budgets. School leaders said their special educational needs (Send) coordinators had worked through the summer to deal with the influx of requests for assessments, as secondary schools say that many more year 7 pupils are arriving with EHCPs or applications. One described the volume of requests as “unreal”, while other schools said they expected to have double the number of incoming pupils with EHCPs when the new academic year begins this month.
/education/2026/oct/04/child-on-child-se.trail: Schools and councils express financial concerns as EHCP applications surge before potential change in provision

/education/2026/oct/04/child-on-child-se.headline: ‘Powerful example’: minister looks to Essex school for blueprint to transform Send provision
/education/2026/oct/04/child-on-child-se.excerpt: Georgia Gould is in a race against time. And the minister responsible for overhauling England’s special educational needs provision is hoping that a state school in Colchester will help her beat the clock. Gould visited Thomas Lord Audley secondary school last week to see the secrets of its success in persuading local parents that it can help children with special needs thrive in a mainstream setting. Under the government’s proprosals announced in February, more funding and universal support are to be given to mainstream schools to accommodate children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Send). The schools minister told the Guardian that institutions such as Thomas Lord Audley are doing many things that will become national policy under the new system. “What they are doing here is a really powerful example of best practice,” Gould said, explaining how the school engages with families and pupils a year or more in advance of entry, and draws up bespoke plans for pupils’ needs similar to the government’s proposed digital records to track and share day-to-day support for children with special needs, called individual support plans. Gould said: “Part of the work we are trying to do, to transform the system towards inclusion, is to take the best practices from schools like this, and make sure that people can see the evidence and the impact they have on things like attendance … And then we want to spread that practice.
/education/2026/oct/04/child-on-child-se.trail: Georgia Gould says moving system towards inclusion will mean parents ‘don’t need to fight’ for support in future

/uk-news/2026/oct/04/women-small-boats-r.headline: Why is the UK-France ‘one in, one out’ migration deal being scrapped?
/uk-news/2026/oct/04/women-small-boats-r.excerpt: The UK government’s “one in, one out” deal with France, which was supposed to help deter small boat arrivals, is expected to expire on Thursday, government sources have said. What was one in, one out? The deal involved returning to France one asylum seeker who had arrived in the UK in a small boat, in exchange for another brought legally to the UK from France. It lasted 423 days – from 10 July 2025 until 1 October 2026. Why didn’t it work out? The UK’s official explanation was that it had not been able to scale up the numbers of asylum seekers involved as much as it would have liked to. However, the scheme was beset with problems. Scores returned to the UK during the scheme because they felt unsafe in France. Some were returned to France a second time while others were allowed to remain in the UK to have their claims processed here. Many were believed to have vanished after being returned to France. Asylum seekers said they were threatened by smugglers because they owed them money and feared being sent back to their home countries or to another European country they had passed through on their journey. How many people were sent back under it and how many returned to the UK? Approximately 1,500 asylum seekers were returned to France, with a similar number brought legally from France to the UK. The numbers removed under the scheme were fewer than the total who arrived in small boats over seven days in the second half of last month.
/uk-news/2026/oct/04/women-small-boats-r.trail: Agreement expected to end on Thursday after running for 423 days, during which it has been beset by problems

/uk-news/2026/oct/04/women-small-boats-r.headline: French court jails six men for manslaughter over mass drowning in Channel
/uk-news/2026/oct/04/women-small-boats-r.excerpt: A Paris court has jailed six ⁠men for manslaughter over the deaths of at least 27 people in the worst mass drowning on record from a small-boat crossing in the Channel. Seven other men were ⁠found guilty of lesser smuggling charges with varying degrees of seriousness, including facilitating illegal immigration as part of ⁠an organised gang and criminal conspiracy. Five years on, another four people are still missing. The court heard that the sinking of an inflatable dinghy in November 2021 was caused by “individuals driven by greed, with utter disregard for human life”. Prosecutors said the convicted men helped launch a “substandard small boat, uncertified, unfit for navigation on the open sea, overcrowded and lacking appropriate lifejackets”. Emmanuel Daoud, a lawyer for one victim’s family, called the proceedings a “trial of greed, cynicism and inhumanity”. Twenty-seven people were confirmed dead when their inflatable dinghy sank in the early hours of 24 November 2021. Four people remain unaccounted for. The victims were mostly Iraqi Kurds, but also included people who were Afghan, Ethiopian, Iranian, Somali, Vietnamese and Egyptian. The youngest known victim was a seven-year-old girl. The confirmed dead included 15 men, seven women and two teenagers. Sentences for the six men found guilty of manslaughter ranged ‌from six to 10 years in prison. For others, sentences ranged from six months suspended to four years in prison.
/uk-news/2026/oct/04/women-small-boats-r.trail: Seven others found guilty of lesser charges in connection to incident in 2021 when inflatable dinghy sank killing at least 27 people with four more still missing

/uk-news/2026/oct/04/women-small-boats-r.headline: Three people dead, including a child, in attempt to cross Channel to UK
/uk-news/2026/oct/04/women-small-boats-r.excerpt: A 10-year-old child and two women died ⁠attempting to cross the Channel on Monday, French authorities have said. Their deaths and the injuries of dozens of others in a large dinghy were probably caused by crushing, according to a French official. France’s maritime police ‌said ‌they received a ‌distress call in the early hours from an inflatable dinghy carrying 105 people that had ‌run into trouble in calm seas. The three passengers were treated onboard but were later confirmed dead by an emergency medical team flown out by helicopter. François-Xavier Lauch, the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, told a press conference: “Apparently there was no drowning, it was likely crushing – which is just as dreadful, especially if we think of the 10-year-old child.” The incident happened off the coast of Wissant, a village about 14 miles (23km) from Calais. A spokesperson for the local prefecture confirmed “a provisional total of three deaths and many more injured”, adding that “sea conditions were calm – the weather is good”. The prefecture described the boat as a “water taxi”, saying it had arrived relatively empty from an inland waterway before picking up passengers from the beach at Wissant. At 10.30am local time (9.30am UK time) six rescue boats were still at the scene searching for people in the water. At least 17 people, including women and children, have died in the Channel this year while attempting to reach the UK.
/uk-news/2026/oct/04/women-small-boats-r.trail: Official says deaths – and dozens of injuries – were probably caused by crushing on boat carrying 105 people

/uk-news/2026/oct/04/women-small-boats-r.headline: UK to open new refugee resettlement routes for Afghan women and Palestinians
/uk-news/2026/oct/04/women-small-boats-r.excerpt: Shabana Mahmood will announce a new legal route for refugees that prioritises Afghan women and girls and Palestinians, unfreezing a scheme that will put the most vulnerable refugees on a faster path to permanent status. The change marks a shift in Mahmood’s approach to asylum seekers after the abrupt closure of the Afghan resettlement scheme last year and changes that will keep refugee status under constant review for two decades. The home secretary is to say the changes will show there is fairness in the immigration system to support the most vulnerable refugees and that a balanced system will “unlock the inherent generosity of this country”. However, immigration experts and refugee charities have said the numbers who will be eligible are too small to deter asylum seekers crossing the Channel in small boats. The reopening of the scheme is likely to attract criticism from the right, especially as women and girls and people with disabilities are the most likely to be dependent on the welfare state. Reform UK and the Conservatives are also likely to raise questions about security checks – which the Home Office says will be carried out – after the Sunday Times revealed that a former Hamas bodyguard had been granted asylum in the UK and was recently arrested on suspicion of being part of a terrorist plot. Mahmood will tell the Labour conference on Monday that she will reopen the UK resettlement scheme, which was in effect suspended for two years, though never formally closed.
/uk-news/2026/oct/04/women-small-boats-r.trail: Exclusive: Move by Shabana Mahmood comes after closure of Afghan scheme last year but experts say numbers too small to deter Channel crossings

/uk-news/2026/oct/04/women-small-boats-r.headline: Ukrainians in UK fear homelessness over host scheme funding cuts
/uk-news/2026/oct/04/women-small-boats-r.excerpt: Ukrainian refugees in the UK fear they could be left homeless after the government quietly axed 70% of funding for hosts of the Homes for Ukraine scheme, reducing monthly “thank you” payments to them from £350 to £100. The scheme was launched after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and has provided support for 181,000 of the 234,000 Ukrainians who have since sought sanctuary in the UK. Now the government has said it will cut the hosting payments and reduce contributions to local authorities, which are paid a sum for each arrival to meet the costs associated with delivering the programme. A written statement to parliament from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) on 15 September said funding would be reduced from £5,900 to £3,300. The changes will come into effect from 1 January 2027. Tetiana, a 73-year-old Ukrainian refugee who has been hosted for two years and four months, said she was devastated to read the government’s letter circulated to hosts in the last few days informing them of the changes. She said: “I feel that this financial change could impact on my host’s ability to host me. If the hosting comes to an end, I don’t know where I will go and how I can start again. I can’t work because of my age and because I have mobility problems. “I fled from Kharkiv, which is close to the Russia frontline, so I can’t go back to Ukraine. I don’t know what I will do. I’m at a loss about what my options will be.
/uk-news/2026/oct/04/women-small-boats-r.trail: Monthly ‘thank you’ payments for people hosting refugees to be cut from £350 to £100 from next year

/world/2026/oct/05/brazil-presidential-r.headline: Polls close in first round of Brazil’s high-stakes presidential election
/world/2026/oct/05/brazil-presidential-r.excerpt: The polls have closed in the first round of Brazil’s highly polarised and high-stakes presidential election that could change not only the direction of Latin America’s largest country but that of the entire region. The election pits the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of Donald Trump and the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup after his failed 2022 re-election attempt. Late on Sunday Bolsonaro was leading Lula in partial results. With results in from almost 65% of the country, Bolsonaro had 49.8% to Lula’s 42.25%, while several other candidates stood in the single digits. Lula and Bolsonaro have alternated as frontrunners in the final stretch, making the outcome unpredictable. In recent days both have focused on persuading undecided voters in hopes of reaching 50% plus one vote; if neither does, there will be a runoff on 25 October. Brazil is one of the few Latin American countries that still has a leftwing government after a wave of rightwing and far-right electoral victories across the region and the US takeover of Venezuela after the capture of Nicolás Maduro. The 80-year-old Lula has positioned himself as one of the last regional leaders still willing to say no to Trump, and has recently accused the US president of trying to interfere in Brazil’s election in Bolsonaro’s favour.
/world/2026/oct/05/brazil-presidential-r.trail: Leftwing incumbent Lula trying to fight off close rival Flávio Bolsonaro, far-right son of jailed ex-president

/world/2026/oct/05/brazil-presidential-r.headline: Brazil’s neck-and-neck election offers test for growing pro-Trump Latin American bloc
/world/2026/oct/05/brazil-presidential-r.excerpt: Shortly after his controversial speech to the United Nations general assembly in September, Donald Trump gathered a dozen like-minded Latin American leaders and boasted that rightwing candidates had won all seven presidential elections held in the region since he began his second term. “Everybody I’ve endorsed has won,” the US president said in New York to most of the leaders of the Shield of the Americas, an anti-drug cartel coalition of 15 countries governed by the right or far right. Those electoral victories – and the US takeover of Venezuela after capturing Nicolás Maduro – have left just six Latin American countries under leftwing governments: regional heavyweights Brazil and Mexico, small Uruguay and Guatemala, and the isolated regimes of Cuba and Nicaragua. On Sunday, Brazilians go to the polls in a presidential election that many believe will determine more than Latin America’s largest country’s fate for the next four years. Given Mexico’s geographic proximity and unique economic relationship with the US, analysts see Brazil as perhaps the last country in the region still capable of saying “no” to Trump’s whims – something that could change dramatically depending on the election result. Polls indicate a neck-and-neck race between Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the 80-year-old leftist incumbent who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, and Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, the far-right senator son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
/world/2026/oct/05/brazil-presidential-r.trail: Sunday’s poll pits the leftist incumbent Lula against the son of a former far-right president convicted of staging a coup

/world/2026/oct/05/brazil-presidential-r.headline: Brazil attorney general says meddling ‘cannot be tolerated’ after Trump funding plans revealed
/world/2026/oct/05/brazil-presidential-r.excerpt: Brazil’s attorney general has said foreign meddling in his country’s institutions and democracy “cannot be tolerated” after a Guardian report revealed how the Trump administration was pushing to direct funds to a campaign against the Brazilian supreme court. Writing on X, Jorge Messias called the report “an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty”. “The information is especially serious in light of Brazil’s electoral process and the recent episodes of external pressure on our institutions,” Messias added. Brazil is three days away from its presidential election – the outcome of which Washington has been accused of trying to influence – where the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, will face off against his far-right rival, the Trump ally Flávio Bolsonaro. The pair are neck and neck in the polls. According to the Brazilian television network GloboNews, the attorney general’s office on Thursday filed a criminal complaint to investigate potential wrongdoing, in response to the Guardian story. Last year, the Trump administration used a campaign of sanctions and tariffs in a failed attempt to pressure Lula’s government and the supreme court over the coup trial of Bolsonaro’s father, the ex-president Jair Bolsonaro. Trump called Bolsonaro’s prosecution a “witch-hunt”, but he was convicted and handed a 27-year sentence for trying to seize power after losing the 2022 election to Lula.
/world/2026/oct/05/brazil-presidential-r.trail: Jorge Messias calls Guardian report ‘an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty’ as nation prepares to go to polls

/world/2026/oct/05/brazil-presidential-r.headline: ‘We’re afraid of dying’: Brazilian news site will not cover upcoming elections after threats
/world/2026/oct/05/brazil-presidential-r.excerpt: Four years ago, during Brazil’s last presidential election, the tyres were slashed on the pickup truck used for reporting by Tapajós de Fato, an independent journalism website in the Brazilian Amazon. Days later, a cat’s severed head was left next to the car park, alongside a note bearing the name of one of the site’s founders, Marcos Wesley Pedroso, and a warning that he would be next. Last July, security cameras outside Pedroso’s house showed cyclists circling the block, whistling and filming his car until, minutes later, another car crashed into it. “I believe they wanted me to come outside so they could ambush me,” said Pedroso. Police have not identified those responsible or established whether the cases are connected, but Pedroso sees them as part of a wider series of threats linked to Tapajós de Fato’s reporting on environmental and Indigenous rights violations, land disputes, and pesticide contamination in the Amazonian state of Pará. As a result, the site’s team decided not to cover this year’s elections – which will choose the next president, state governors, members of the lower house and part of the senate, with the first round on 4 October. “We’re afraid of dying and of putting our families’ safety at risk,” said Pedroso. He added that the site, whose name refers to the 1,238-mile-long (1,992km) Tapajós River, would remain online and continue covering environmental issues, but would avoid stories about the election.
/world/2026/oct/05/brazil-presidential-r.trail: Co-founder of independent website Tapajós de Fato said decision was made to protect journalists and their families

/world/2026/oct/05/brazil-presidential-r.headline: ‘Viscerally dedicated to social issues’: behind Lula’s drive to win final term in Brazil’s crunch election
/world/2026/oct/05/brazil-presidential-r.excerpt: On 1 January 2023, a few hours after being sworn in for his third stint as Brazil’s president, a ravenous Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva sneaked away from a celebratory cocktail party packed with politicians and diplomats to grab a snack with one of his oldest friends. “This is your penultimate term,” that friend, the Dominican theologian and writer Frei Betto, recalls telling Lula as the pair chewed the fat in a back room of the foreign ministry in Brasília. Betto says Lula laughed off his provocation, insisting: “No, Betto! It’s the last one. I’m done!” But the theologian was unconvinced. “I’m certain that in four years’ time you’ll stand for a fourth,” he assured the leftwing veteran during their 40-minute tête-à-tête. “And sure enough, he did,” Betto added last month, as his forecast came true. On 4 October, just a few weeks shy of his 81st birthday, Lula will indeed seek to extend his legendary five-decade career in what will be the former union leader’s seventh presidential election since his first in 1989. Lula ran three unsuccessful campaigns before finally making history as Brazil’s first elected working-class president in 2002 and winning re-election in 2006. In 2022 he staged a sensational comeback, defeating the far-right incumbent, Jair Bolsonaro, before thwarting a coup attempt masterminded by his rival a week into his third term.
/world/2026/oct/05/brazil-presidential-r.trail: Longtime friend tells of president’s obsession with social justice and fears for country’s future under another Bolsonaro presidency

/business/2026/oct/05/strikes-by-north-s.headline: The truth behind Donald Trump’s ‘biggest oil deal in world history’
/business/2026/oct/05/strikes-by-north-s.excerpt: Donald Trump has long coveted the oilfields of other nations and declared an agreement with Venezuela to be “the biggest oil deal in world history”. But the agreement, reached after the US seized Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro, is almost certainly doomed to collapse amid a wide array of legal and logistical issues, a Guardian investigation has found. The US president first mused about taking oil from Iran in 1987, when he told ABC’s Barbara Walters that Iranian attacks on American shipping during the Iran-Iraq war required an extreme response. “Why couldn’t we go in and take over some of their oil, which is along the sea?” he asked. Over the ensuing years, he has returned frequently to the idea that the US should seize oil from other countries after military conflict, from Libya to Iraq. Earlier this year, Trump finally got a chance to enact his plan – at gunpoint. US forces stormed Venezuela in January and seized Maduro, who was quickly shuttled to a federal holding facility in the US and replaced by the compliant Delcy Rodríguez. Trump told the Atlantic in the days following the raid: “If [Rodríguez] doesn’t do what’s right, she is going to pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro.” Then in August, Trump announced that the office of strategic capital (OSC) at the Pentagon, which he has rapidly transformed, would own a third of the second-biggest private Venezuelan oil firm, North American Blue Energy Partners (Nabep).
/business/2026/oct/05/strikes-by-north-s.trail: The US’s oil deal with Venezuela faces multiple legal and logistical problems, including questions about whether it can be implemented

/business/2026/oct/05/strikes-by-north-s.headline: Record fuel prices across EU prompt calls for bloc-wide windfall tax on firms
/business/2026/oct/05/strikes-by-north-s.excerpt: European governments have discussed imposing a bloc-wide windfall tax on energy companies, as near-record fuel and gas prices pile pressure on leaders desperate to contain mounting public discontent and the challenge of the far right. With elections due next year in eight EU countries including France, Italy, Spain and Poland, leaders are scrambling to head off the potential fallout from what analysts have warned could be one of the continent’s biggest energy shocks in decades. Germany’s finance minister, Lars Klingbeil, called on ‌the European Commission at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday to propose possible ways to tax what he described as the excessive profits of oil companies. “Several member states have been calling for models for a long time,” Klingbeil said, demanding proposals by next month. “People can see how oil companies are exploiting the situation, overcharging and significantly increasing their profits.” Oil futures have climbed back above $100 a ⁠barrel, about 50% higher than before the Iran war, as escalating attacks across the Middle East threaten more supply routes. Derivatives markets suggest traders do not ‌expect a near-term drop in ‌prices. Pump prices have already reached all-time highs across Europe. In Germany, diesel prices surged to a record average of €2.45 a litre on Wednesday, while petrol hit a fresh high of €2.31 a litre, according to Europe’s largest motoring association, ADAC.
/business/2026/oct/05/strikes-by-north-s.trail: German minister says companies are ‘exploiting situation’ in Middle East, as sky-high prices become major domestic issue for leaders

/business/2026/oct/05/strikes-by-north-s.headline: US borrowing costs hit 5% for first time since 2023 amid bond sell-off
/business/2026/oct/05/strikes-by-north-s.excerpt: US government borrowing costs have risen to 5% for the first time since 2023 as soaring oil prices fuelled by the war in the Middle East trigger an intensifying sell-off in the global bond market. The yield – in effect the interest rate – on 10-year US Treasury bonds hit the psychologically important threshold on Monday, on a day of renewed selling pressure on Wall Street as the global oil price reached $108 a barrel. With traders awaiting a crunch US Federal Reserve interest rate decision on Wednesday, the benchmark rate has steadily climbed from a low this year of 4% before the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran in late February. The yield was last above 5% in October 2023. It comes as the rising global oil price stokes inflation fears, with the latest move prompted by a series of drone attacks that have forced Saudi Arabia to close a vital east-west crude pipeline as the fallout from the war mounts. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, surged to more than $108.5 a barrel on Monday – a 3.7% increase on the day. The spike came after Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi forces launched several attacks against Saudi Arabia and captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait on Sunday, expanding their control of the waterway.
/business/2026/oct/05/strikes-by-north-s.trail: Soaring oil prices of above $108 a barrel after Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure stoke inflation fears

/business/2026/oct/05/strikes-by-north-s.headline: Africa’s richest man aiming to make $23bn from continent’s biggest-ever IPO
/business/2026/oct/05/strikes-by-north-s.excerpt: The fortune of Africa’s richest person could swell by two thirds to nearly $60bn (£44bn) after his refinery in Nigeria listed publicly in the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering. If Monday’s flotation of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals on the Nigerian exchange goes to plan, then Aliko Dangote will add a further $23bn (£17bn) to his $35bn net worth. Dangote, who has framed the offering as “an IPO for the people”, hopes it will draw in a broad mix of institutional and retail investors with a minimum subscription of just 10 shares at a cost of 5,250 naira (£2.94). The share purchases have a month to complete, with the process finishing on 13 October. The IPO has been marketed to young Nigerians in particular, through banking platforms and fintech ventures, as a way of building wealth and growing the economy. If completely subscribed, the refinery’s value is expected to rise to about 65.22tn naira (£36.5bn). That would be a big win for Dangote, who has financed several successful presidential campaigns in Nigeria, where policymakers have granted him a near monopoly in his chosen sectors. Responding last year to criticism of his political influence, he said: “We have chosen to build here, to employ here, to produce here. Let us not use the cry of monopoly to stall growth. No one is prevented from investing.” Dangote, 69, made his fortune in cement and sugar.
/business/2026/oct/05/strikes-by-north-s.trail: Public offering of Aliko Dangote’s Nigerian oil refinery business could swell his net wealth by two-thirds

/business/2026/oct/05/strikes-by-north-s.headline: BP seeks to end years of boardroom turmoil with appointment of new chair
/business/2026/oct/05/strikes-by-north-s.excerpt: BP has appointed a new chair after a months-long search triggered by the controversial ousting of Albert Manifold, seeking to draw a line under years of boardroom turmoil at the UK oil and gas company. Ian Tyler, who has served as the interim chair and has sat on the BP board as a non-executive director since April 2025, will assume the role on a permanent basis immediately. His appointment comes after Manifold’s shock removal in late May after only eight months in the role, with BP citing “serious concerns” about his tenure. Amanda Blanc, BP’s senior independent director who led the search for a new chair and also runs the insurer Aviva as chief executive, announced on Wednesday she would stand down at next year’s annual meeting. She was criticised after Manifold’s short tenure as chair, because she had led the process that led to his appointment to replace Helge Lund. When Manifold left, Blanc said he had helped drive BP’s transformation but there had been “governance oversight and conduct issues” which the board deemed unacceptable. Reports claimed senior colleagues had felt belittled by Manifold. He was also accused of aggressive behaviour and acting as if he had been an executive rather than a chair. Manifold responded by accusing the company of firing him without warning and disputed reports about his conduct.
/business/2026/oct/05/strikes-by-north-s.trail: Ian Tyler, already in role on an interim basis, is tasked with shifting strategy to refocus on fossil fuel extraction

/money/2026/oct/05/scammers-hijacking-uk.headline: ‘We noticed a login from a new device’: the message from fraudsters targeting your X account
/money/2026/oct/05/scammers-hijacking-uk.excerpt: You have had an X account for years, since it was known as Twitter. When an email arrives about a new login from a location nowhere near where you live, alarm bells begin to ring. “We noticed a login to your account from a new device. Was this you?” the email asks. The location is Arizona, but you live in London. The device is “Firefox Desktop on Mac”. “If this wasn’t you,” the email continues, “complete these steps now to protect your account.” The steps include clicking a link to change your password, which will end up with you “logged out of all your active X sessions except the one you’re using at this time” and to click another link to review the apps that have access to your account and revoke any that are unfamiliar. The steps are legitimate advice from X, but the links to reset your password, or to review app access are not. The email is fake and attempting to trick you into giving scammers your password, or direct access to your X account. “Scammers want your X username and password, or to trick you into approving a malicious link that gives them access to your account without needing your password,” says Jake Moore, a global cybersecurity adviser at ESET. Once the criminals have access to your account they will more than likely use it to attempt to commit further fraud including crypto scams, phishing attacks and misinformation campaigns. What it looks like The fake emails are almost an exact replica of legitimate login notifications sent by X.
/money/2026/oct/05/scammers-hijacking-uk.trail: They are out to steal your password to commit further fraud such as crypto scams or phishing attacks
